title: RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M against clinical malaria: vaccine-specific efficacy on the log scale, with the estimand and the follow-up window stated on every row
question: For each of the two malaria vaccines separately, what is the efficacy against clinical malaria across the randomised cohorts that report the SAME EFFECT MEASURE for clinical malaria, aligned on every dimension the sources permit and crossing the rest with each difference named on the pool that crosses it -- and where does that differ from the published synthesis of the same literature? The question does NOT claim these cohorts estimate identical quantities. Each pool records whether they do, and neither of them does.
question_note: This question has been wrong in both directions and the history is kept because it is the more useful thing to read. It said SAME ESTIMAND while the tables recorded differences; it was then widened to say the pools AVERAGE ACROSS those differences, and a reviewer was right that widening the question widened the CLAIM instead of answering the objection. What answered it was going back to the sources: the phase 3 trial reports its younger age band separately, at the seasonal sites, on the same MEASURE and the same window, so that band is what the pool now uses and the age mismatch is gone rather than excused. The differences that REMAIN are real and are named on the pool. Earlier text follows. This question said SAME ESTIMAND until a reviewer set it beside the object's own uniformity tables, which record an age range that differs, a case definition that differs and, on the other pool, a follow-up window that differs. Two things cannot both be true, and it was the question that was wrong: what these pools produce is an AVERAGE ACROSS those differences, which is a legitimate thing to publish and a different thing from what was claimed. The differences are recorded on every pool, tested by leave-one-out, and now named in the question itself so a reader meets them before meeting the number. An earlier version of this question required cohorts to report over the same follow-up WINDOW as well. That was a rule invented here, it was stricter than the Cochrane Handbook, and it was wrong in a way that cost something: it would have discarded a pool of two cohorts sharing the effect measure, the regression model, the case definition, the age band, the dosing schedule and the comparator CLASS -- differing on the points its uniformity table records, none of which is the effect MEASURE, though one of them -- the crossed follow-up window -- IS an estimand difference, because this object defines the window inside the estimand and the pool records it as one -- with no detectable statistical heterogeneity, purely because one reported a median follow-up and the other a fixed endpoint two months later. What each pool holds constant is recorded in one place, its table, and is not restated here beyond that pointer. The Handbook states which effect measure suits which data type (sections 10.8 and 10.9), that clinical and methodological diversity is to be DOCUMENTED rather than assumed away (section 10.10.1), and that influential or unclear decisions are to be tested by sensitivity analysis (section 10.14). It does NOT supply a sufficiency test that makes same-measure-plus-low-heterogeneity enough on its own: whether studies are similar enough to combine is left to the review authors. An earlier version of this note called that combination 'the Handbook's test', which was an overclaim and is withdrawn. The judgement here is OURS -- recorded dimension by dimension, tested by leave-one-out, and open to a reader who weighs it differently. Both review families flagged the old wording as inconsistent with the object's practice, and they were right that the two disagreed; the wording is what was wrong.
_prose_rule: Every text field is PROSE unless it is on the validator's numeric list. Prose may not restate a number the object holds structurally; it references it instead, so a sentence cannot go stale against the field it describes.
_sourcing_rule: Every MEASURED input names the source layer it came from and carries the verbatim sentence it was read from. An effect on the log scale carries the published efficacy or ratio it was derived from, so the derivation is checkable rather than asserted.
_estimand_rule: No pooled estimate may combine rows whose estimand identifiers differ. An endpoint analysed as a time to an event, or as a rate over person-time, may not be stored as a table of participants with and without an event. No two rows sharing a control group may contribute to the same pool. These are enforced by the validator, not by convention.
completeness_statement: FULL BUILD: every randomised cohort this object cites, it holds and reports. Nothing was cited and dropped, so there is no removal block and no quarantine. Cohorts are counted at the level of the RANDOMISATION; the further reports set aside are listed on the deduplication decision. Eligibility is stated in the question. Source depth is not uniform and each source entry names its own layer.

SCOPE:cohort-level-deduplication.conformance: Section 4.6.1 is titled 'Studies (not reports) as the unit of interest' and states that reviews have studies as the primary units of interest and analysis, and that a single study may have more than one report about it. Section 4.6.2 covers identifying multiple reports of one study and associating them with each other. The cohorts here whose further reports were identified and set aside are named in the list beside this record, each contributing one row; the count is read off that list rather than stated, because a hand-written count of them was wrong in review and understated it. An earlier version of this record cited 10.10.1 for this, which is the definition of heterogeneity and does not govern the unit of interest at all.

SCOPE:shared-control-relevant-groups.decision: Where one control group serves several published contrasts, determine which intervention group is RELEVANT to the outcome being estimated, use that contrast, and report the others outside every pool
SCOPE:shared-control-relevant-groups.conformance: Section 23.3.4 is explicit that entering several comparisons so that the same comparator group appears more than once double-counts those participants and creates a unit-of-analysis error, which is what makes some choice compulsory here. It then offers four ways to make it: combine groups, select one pair, split the shared group, or undertake a network meta-analysis -- and it says of selecting one pair that it loses information and is open to results-related choices, so is NOT generally recommended. That caveat is quoted here rather than omitted, because a reviewer raised it. The reason it does not bite is that this is not an arbitrary selection under 23.3.4: it is a relevance determination under 23.3.2, 'Determining which intervention groups are relevant'. Each affected trial randomised groups that are DIFFERENT INTERVENTIONS -- a boosted against an unboosted schedule, two adjuvant doses, four dosing schedules, a vaccine against a vaccine-plus-chemoprevention combination -- and each pooled outcome names ONE of them in its own definition. Combining them, the section's first-listed option, would create a schedule no participant received and would defeat the regimen separation this object exists to maintain. INFORMATION IS LOST FROM THE POOLED ESTIMATE and this object does not claim otherwise: a contrast shown under carried contrasts is visible to a reader and contributes nothing to the pooled value. An earlier version did claim otherwise, and a reviewer was right to say that displaying a contrast elsewhere is not the same as its informing the estimate. What is claimed is narrower -- that the loss is not ARBITRARY, because each excluded arm is a different intervention from the one its outcome names, and that it is not concealed. Splitting the shared group remains available and would change the estimate; it is not used because the groups are not interchangeable doses of one intervention.

SCOPE:active-comparator-not-an-efficacy.decision: Do not express a head-to-head ratio against an active comparator as a vaccine efficacy
SCOPE:active-comparator-not-an-efficacy.conformance: Section 3.2.3, 'Defining which comparisons will be made', distinguishes intervention-versus-placebo and intervention-versus-control from intervention A versus intervention B. The chemoprevention trial is the third kind, and the quantity it estimates is therefore not commensurate with the others: one minus a ratio against an effective comparator is not an efficacy against an unprotected control, and reporting it as one would describe a vaccine that barely works where the trial found two interventions performing alike. The row carries the published ratio and no efficacy percentage, and the validator blocks one being added. This too previously cited 10.10.1, which does not govern comparison definition.

methodological_authority.version_checked_how: The publisher's versions-and-changes page was read, and it is what settles which version is current: it lists 6.5.1 as the newest release line, with entries dated 2026 and 2025, above 6.5 dated 2024. Where they conflict this object follows the version history and the per-chapter citation lines, because those are the more specific and the more recent statements.

methodological_authority.scope_of_this_rule: Every decision about pooling, scope, estimand, heterogeneity or unit of analysis in this object names the section that governs it. A decision with no cited section is a preference wearing the clothes of a method.
methodological_authority.where_the_decisions_live: Each decision, the sections governing it and the conformance argument are attached to the result they govern, under its handbook block. They were also copied here and the copy is removed: the same text in two places is the defect this object has spent six rounds removing.
methodological_authority.note: Where this object had to decide whether something could be combined, the decision was referred to the Handbook rather than to a rule invented here. The sections relied on are listed with what each one settled, so a reader can check the reasoning against the source rather than against this object's own assertion of it.

sections_relied_on.title: Defining which comparisons will be made
sections_relied_on.used_for: Distinguishes intervention-versus-placebo and intervention-versus-control from intervention A versus intervention B. The chemoprevention trial is the third kind, which is why its ratio is never reported as an efficacy.

sections_relied_on.title: Studies (not reports) as the unit of interest
sections_relied_on.used_for: Reviews have STUDIES as the unit of analysis and a single study may have several reports. This is the authority for counting cohorts rather than publications.

sections_relied_on.title: Identifying multiple reports from the same study
sections_relied_on.used_for: Associating the several reports of one cohort with each other. The cohorts this was done for are listed on the deduplication decision itself; no count is restated here, because the count restated here was wrong twice.

sections_relied_on.title: Determining which intervention groups are relevant
sections_relied_on.used_for: The governing rule where a trial randomised more than two groups: which of them the review's own question concerns. Each pooled outcome names one regimen, and that is what selects the arm.

sections_relied_on.title: How to include multiple groups from one study
sections_relied_on.used_for: Its prohibition on entering the same comparator group more than once, which it calls a unit-of-analysis error -- the reason a choice is compulsory here. Its four options, and its caveat against arbitrary pair-selection, are both recorded on the decision rather than omitted.

sections_relied_on.title: Meta-analysis of counts and rates
sections_relied_on.used_for: Establishes the RATE RATIO as the effect measure for count and rate data, combined as log rate ratios by the generic inverse-variance method. This is the measure and the method used for the RTS,S pooled result.

sections_relied_on.title: Meta-analysis of time-to-event outcomes
sections_relied_on.used_for: Establishes the HAZARD RATIO as the effect measure for time-to-event data, combined as log hazard ratios by the same generic method. This is the measure and method used for the R21 pooled result -- and it is a DIFFERENT measure from the one in section 10.8, which is why the two vaccines' results are not combined with each other.

sections_relied_on.title: Combining dichotomous and continuous outcomes
sections_relied_on.used_for: Read as the limiting case rather than as permission. Where the Handbook sanctions combining unlike measures it names the conversion; it provides one between odds ratios and standardised mean differences, and none between a hazard ratio and a rate ratio.

sections_relied_on.title: What is heterogeneity?
sections_relied_on.used_for: The distinction between clinical and methodological diversity on one hand and statistical heterogeneity on the other. Differences in follow-up length and in the fever criterion are documented as diversity rather than treated as disqualifying.

sections_relied_on.title: Identifying and measuring heterogeneity
sections_relied_on.used_for: The I-squared bands. Both pooled results here fall in the lowest band; the cross-vaccine combination that was removed fell in the highest.

sections_relied_on.title: Strategies for addressing heterogeneity
sections_relied_on.used_for: Its strategy 'do not do a meta-analysis', on the stated grounds that where results vary considerably an average may mislead. This is the authority for removing the cross-vaccine pooled figure. An earlier version called it the section's FIRST-listed strategy; it is not. The section opens with 'Check again that the data are correct', and a review leg was right about the order. The chapter was reopened to confirm it before the claim was withdrawn, because that leg has been wrong about section content before and a track record is not evidence either way.

sections_relied_on.title: Investigating heterogeneity
sections_relied_on.used_for: Subgroup analysis as what REPLACES a combined estimate that should not be computed. Its subsection on whether the effect differs between subgroups says a FORMAL statistical approach SHOULD be used where subgroups are compared, and warns against comparing within-subgroup inferences such as P values. It does NOT ask that subgroups be left untested, and an earlier version of this entry said it did -- a reviewer called that a misrepresentation and was right. The strata here are reported and not compared for a reason that section supplies no remedy for: they carry DIFFERENT effect measures, a hazard ratio against a rate ratio, and the test it describes is a heterogeneity test across subgroup results, which presumes one measure. The comparison is declined because it cannot be made validly, NOT because the Handbook asks for it to be declined. This section is also NOT the authority for dropping the combined figure -- that is 10.10.3, and the two are easy to confuse.

sections_relied_on.title: Introduction to meta-analysis
sections_relied_on.used_for: What a meta-analysis IS -- the combination of results across studies -- and therefore why a row that only one cohort reports over its window is presented alone. It is cited where a measure-specific section would once have been: an earlier version cited the rate-ratio section beside a row that expressly declines to call its measure a rate ratio, and a reviewer was right that a section cannot govern a measure the row refuses to claim.

sections_relied_on.title: Incorporating heterogeneity into random-effects models
sections_relied_on.used_for: The choice of a random-effects model AND of the estimator for the between-study variance. The effect-measure sections do not govern either, which a reviewer pointed out. Its subsections carry the record that other estimators perform better than DerSimonian and Laird, which is why the headline here is restricted maximum likelihood, and the advice to compare the methods when there are only two or three studies. An earlier version of this sentence said 'better than the one kept here', which was true when DerSimonian and Laird was the headline and became false the moment it stopped being; a reviewer caught the remnant.

sections_relied_on.title: Sensitivity analyses
sections_relied_on.used_for: The requirement that a pooled result be shown robust to influential decisions. Both pooled outcomes carry a leave-one-out analysis testing the decision that was challenged in review.

screening.search_note: Candidate records were retrieved from PubMed across both vaccines and screened against the eligibility boundary stated in the question. The published synthesis this object reconciles against was used as a search prior and a completeness check, not as a source of trials.
screening.eligibility: A randomised controlled trial of RTS,S/AS01 or R21/Matrix-M reporting a clinical malaria efficacy result against a control group. Counted at the level of the randomised COHORT, not the publication.

excluded.reason: A different adjuvant formulation of the same antigen
excluded.detail: Field trials of the earlier AS02 adjuvant systems fall outside the boundary in the question, which names the AS01 formulation. This is a scope decision and a reader may disagree with it; it is recorded rather than left implicit.

excluded.reason: A further publication of a cohort already included
excluded.detail: Several cohorts here were reported more than once as follow-up lengthened. Each contributes ONE row, from the report this object cites. Counting the others would enter one randomised cohort into a synthesis several times, which is the unit-of-analysis error this object exists to avoid.

excluded.reason: An ancillary or secondary analysis of an included cohort
excluded.detail: Genotypic, immunological and modelling analyses of cohorts already included are not separate trials and carry no separate efficacy contrast against a control.

Reviews and commentaries retrieved by the search.

screening.known_limitation: The screening was done from titles, abstracts and, where needed, full text, on records this search retrieved. A search is not a census, and no claim is made that no eligible cohort exists outside it. What is claimed is narrower and checkable: every cohort this object cites, it holds and reports, and every exclusion above is stated with its reason.

reconciliation.access_limitation: The publisher's full text was not retrievable, so this comparison rests on the review's abstract and its institutional repository record. Where a statement below concerns the review's METHODS rather than its reported numbers, it is stated as what those numbers imply and not as a finding read from a methods section.

matches.detail: The review reports a number of included studies equal to the number of distinct randomised COHORTS this object located independently. This is recorded because it is true, NOT because it establishes anything: two sets of the same size can have different members, and the review's included-study list was not in the material that could be retrieved. It is a coincidence of counts until that list can be read, and the unresolved section below says so.

matches.item: Direction and rough magnitude for R21
matches.detail: The review describes this vaccine as showing high efficacy, which agrees with this object's pooled seasonal result.

The review reports that protective efficacy declined over time, and this object does not contradict it. An earlier version of this entry went further and said this object's own rows demonstrate the same pattern, because the longest follow-up carried the smallest estimate. That was withdrawn on review: it is not true of these rows. The longest follow-up row is neither the smallest efficacy here -- the infant cohort at a shorter follow-up is smaller -- nor the smallest ratio. These rows differ from one another in vaccine, estimand, age and window all at once, so the variation between them cannot be attributed to follow-up length, and a cross-sectional read of them is not evidence of waning. Waning is a within-cohort question, and the trials that answer it do so inside their own reports rather than in this comparison.

corrections.item: A single pooled risk ratio for BOTH vaccines together
corrections.review_reports: One risk ratio presented as covering both vaccines in the older age group.
corrections.this_object: Refused as a primary result. The two vaccines' pivotal trials do not report the same quantity: one reports a hazard ratio for the time to a first episode over a year, the other a negative-binomial rate ratio for all episodes over its whole follow-up. A single ratio across both is a weighted average of two different estimands. This object reports each vaccine separately and carries NO combined figure at all. An earlier version of this sentence said the combined figure was confined to an outcome declared exploratory; that outcome no longer carries a pooled point, an interval or an efficacy percentage, because the gate removed them, so the sentence had gone stale against the object it describes.

corrections.item: Ordinary binary risk ratios for time-to-event and rate endpoints
corrections.review_reports: Risk ratios, the effect measure of a table of participants with and without an event.
corrections.this_object: Both pivotal trials analysed something else. One used Cox regression on the time to a first episode; the other used negative binomial regression on all episodes with person-time as the offset, so its published counts are EPISODES and exceed the number of participants. Treating either as a table of participants changes the estimand and, for the episode counts, uses a numerator that cannot sit over a participant denominator at all. This object stores every effect on the log scale with its standard error derived from the published interval, and its validator blocks a survival or rate endpoint stored as a binary one.

corrections.item: An event rate reported as though it were a vaccine efficacy
corrections.review_reports: An event rate quoted for R21 alongside the efficacy discussion, in the words the staged record gives and no more.
corrections.this_object: Not carried in any form. The staged abstract and repository record call it a low event rate and do not say what it is a rate OF, over what denominator, or in which arm, so there is not enough there to treat it as a contrast and it is not used as one. An earlier version of this entry asserted it was a single-arm proportion with no comparator in it. That may well be right, but the staged record does not say so, and a correction that over-reads its source is the fault it is correcting.

unresolved.detail: Both pivotal programmes publish more than one contrast against a SHARED control group, and both were published more than once at different follow-up points. A review that counts publications rather than randomised cohorts, or that uses more than one contrast per shared control, would double-count control participants. Whether this review did either cannot be determined from the material that was retrievable. This object makes the corresponding choice explicit on every row: contrasts sharing a control carry the same control key, one is chosen, and the rest are carried outside every pool.

unresolved.item: Which R21 figure entered an age-banded analysis
unresolved.detail: The review reports analysing an age band matching the older RTS,S cohort. The R21 phase 3 enrolled a WIDER band extending beyond it, and found efficacy to differ significantly by age within its own population, so the trial's overall figure and its figure for the narrower band are not the same number. Which of the two a reader of the review is seeing therefore matters. An earlier draft of this reconciliation asserted that the review had used the wider trial's overall figure; that assertion is WITHDRAWN, because the review also publishes the narrower band as its analysis population and the trial publishes a subgroup for exactly that band, so the review could legitimately have extracted the subgroup. Without the included-study table there is no basis to say which it did, and saying so anyway would be the same kind of over-claim this object criticises elsewhere. What is recorded instead is the fact that makes the question live, and this object's own response to it: every row here states its own population rather than being aligned to a common band.

handbook.decision: POOL two cohorts reporting the same effect measure for the same outcome concept, producing an AVERAGE ACROSS documented differences in analysis population, case definition, comparator
handbook.conformance: Section 10.9 gives the hazard ratio as the effect measure for time-to-event data and sanctions combining log hazard ratios by generic inverse-variance. Both cohorts report a Cox hazard ratio for the time to a first episode over the same window against a rabies control. What the pool crosses is in the uniformity table, documented under 10.10.1; heterogeneity is in the lowest band of 10.10.2; the inclusion decision is tested under 10.14. AGE IS NO LONGER CROSSED BY THIS POOL. The wider trial reports its own efficacy as significantly higher in the younger band than the older one, so age is an effect modifier on its own evidence, and an earlier version of this pool set that trial's ALL-AGE seasonal figure against a cohort that enrolled only the younger band. A review leg objected in three consecutive rounds and was right. The trial reports the younger band separately, at the seasonal sites, on the same MEASURE over the same window, so the pool now uses that row and both cohorts are the same age band. Section 10.10.1 asks that a synthesis be undertaken only where the review authors JUDGE the studies sufficiently similar to give a meaningful summary. That judgement is now a much easier one to make and it is still ours to make: what the pool still crosses is analysis population, case definition and comparator product, each named with its reason on the uniformity table, and none of them is a modifier the sources report an effect for. Section 10.10.4 is what governs the MODEL and the between-study variance estimator, which the effect-measure sections above do not: it records that estimators other than DerSimonian and Laird perform better and that restricted maximum likelihood is now the default in the Cochrane software, and its subsection on few studies advises comparing the methods when there are only two or three. This pool has two, so that comparison is done and sits in the sensitivity block. An earlier version of this object cited only the effect-measure and heterogeneity sections for a decision they do not govern, and a reviewer was right to say so.

r21_seasonal_first_12m.estimand_id_means: the estimand of the POOLED value, which is the average this result reports. It is NOT a claim that the contributing cohorts estimate identical quantities. The dimensions on which they differ are listed in the uniformity table below, and the pooled value averages across them.

estimand_family: Both trials state efficacy as one minus a hazard ratio: 'Vaccine efficacy was calculated as 1 minus the hazard ratio (HR)' appears in each.
regression_model: Both name Cox: 'Cox regression models were used to analyse first episodes of clinical malaria' and 'The primary analysis was time to first episode of clinical malaria and was analysed by Cox regression'.
follow_up_window: Both report a twelve-month analysis, and they are the same NOMINAL length rather than the same measured one: one states 'Primary analyses of vaccine efficacy were based on 12 months of follow-up' while the other states 'Efficacy was further assessed at 12 months (range 329-369 days) after the third vaccination'. The range is recorded because a reader should see that one trial's twelve months is a spread of days.
analysis_population: one cohort analysed a modified per-protocol population and the other a modified intention-to-treat population, which that trial states is equivalent to per-protocol because every participant received the correct vaccine
case_definition: BOTH require parasitaemia above the same density, and both require fever -- but the later trial also accepts a REPORTED history of fever in the preceding day where the earlier one requires a measured temperature. The later definition is therefore slightly the broader of the two, which would if anything admit milder episodes into both arms of that trial. It is documented as clinical diversity under Handbook section 10.10.1 rather than corrected, because neither trial can be reanalysed under the other's definition
comparator: both control groups received a rabies vaccine, so the comparator is of the same INACTIVE class and neither control was protected against malaria -- but they are not the same PRODUCT. One cohort's control was Rabivax-S from the Serum Institute of India and the other's was Abhayrab from Indian Immunologicals. An earlier version of this row read identical, which hid that difference under a word the staged sources do not support; a reviewer read both trial reports and found the product names. Neither product confers malaria protection, so the difference is documented under 10.10.1 rather than treated as disqualifying
age_range: Both rows are the 5-17 month band. The phase 2b cohort enrolled it outright -- "Participants aged 5-17 months were recruited" -- and the phase 3 row is now the subgroup that trial reports separately for exactly that band: "the younger age group had the highest 12-month vaccine efficacy on time to first clinical malaria episode at seasonal (79% [95% CI 73-84])". An earlier version of this pool used that trial's ALL-AGE seasonal figure against a 5-17 month cohort, which is the mismatch this re-extraction removes.
control_group_separation: Each trial randomised its OWN control group and neither shares control participants with the other: 'group 3, the control group, received rabies vaccinations' and 'randomly assigned (2:1) to receive 5 ug R21 plus 50 ug Matrix-M or a control vaccine'.

r21_seasonal_first_12m.poolable_reason: Identical across the contributing cohorts: estimand family, regression model, follow up window, age range, control group separation. NOT identical, and pooled anyway with the reason recorded against each: analysis population, case definition, comparator. A pooled value across a dimension that differs is only as good as the reason given for crossing it, and those reasons are on this block rather than in a sentence that could go stale against them.

heterogeneity.tau2_estimator: REML -- copied from this block's declared `estimator`, which is the authoritative record of how the pool was computed. NOT inferred: an object that declared no estimator would be left undeclared here, because the absence is itself the finding.
heterogeneity.i2_definition: UNDECIDABLE from this object. I-squared is 0 and Q is below the degrees of freedom, where the Higgins form is negative-and-clamped and the REML/metafor form is exactly zero -- BOTH DEFINITIONS GIVE 0 and nothing here distinguishes them. Recorded as undecidable rather than guessed.

r21_seasonal_first_12m.heterogeneity_status: tau-squared and I-squared are recorded beside this line.

sensitivity.authority: Cochrane Handbook version 6, section 10.14: sensitivity analyses examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions.
sensitivity.decision_under_test: whether the pooled estimate depends on including cohorts that differ on analysis population, case definition, comparator -- the dimensions this pool crosses, each recorded with its reason in the uniformity table above

between_study_variance_method_comparison.why: Section 10.10.4.4 records that estimators other than DerSimonian and Laird perform better and that restricted maximum likelihood is now the default in the Cochrane software, and section 10.10.4.5 advises comparing the methods in a sensitivity analysis when there are only two or three studies. This pool has two. A reviewer was right that an earlier version cited neither section for a decision they govern and did not run the comparison they ask for.
between_study_variance_method_comparison.verdict: The variance estimators move the summary very little, which is what the Handbook reports is usual. The interval method is the axis that matters with two studies, and section 10.10.4.5 states its own caveat plainly: with two or three studies the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman interval is liable to be far too wide while the ordinary one is liable to be too narrow. Both are printed and neither is treated as decisive.
between_study_variance_method_comparison.estimator_kept: The headline estimator is restricted maximum likelihood, which section 10.10.4.4 records as the default in the Cochrane software and as better supported than DerSimonian and Laird. An earlier version kept DerSimonian and Laird and gave as its reason that the local validator could recompute it -- software convenience presented as Handbook conformance, which a reviewer called out on this object and on another in the same batch. The tooling moved instead of the method: the validator now recomputes restricted maximum likelihood independently. DerSimonian and Laird is shown beside it and moves the summary barely at all.

sensitivity.conclusion: Omitting either cohort moves the estimate by at most 0.0133 on the ratio scale. The pooled value is not carried by one cohort, and neither single-cohort estimate contradicts it.

r21_seasonal_first_12m.poolable_DEPRECATED_note: `poolable` MEANT ONLY 'the source page pooled these trials'. It was never a judgement that the pool was sound, and the renderer read it as permission to assert 'pooled on the X scale'. RENAMED to source_page_pooled, which is what it says. `poolable` is retained so nothing breaks, and it is DEPRECATED: read source_page_pooled for what the source did, and estimand_established for whether the pool is defensible. A PAGE SHOULD DISPLAY A POOLED ESTIMATE BECAUSE ITS ESTIMAND WAS ESTABLISHED, NOT BECAUSE SOMEONE ONCE POOLED IT.
r21_seasonal_first_12m.estimand_established_means: TRUE only where every contributing trial has been READ and shown to measure the same quantity, or the same construct with a variance stated. FALSE where that was checked and failed. NULL where it was never checked -- AN ABSENT ASSERTION AND A NEGATIVE ONE ARE DIFFERENT STATES and null is not a pass.

house_rule_interval_2026_08_18.estimator: REML with Hartung-Knapp, t on k-1 = 1 degree(s) of freedom (t = 12.7062)
house_rule_interval_2026_08_18.THE_POINT_ESTIMATE_IS_UNCHANGED: The published point is 0.2167 and the house-rule point is 0.2167. THE NUMBER A READER REMEMBERS DOES NOT MOVE; what differs is the precision claim. That is why nothing downstream catches this -- every memorable quantity survives.
house_rule_interval_2026_08_18.variance_inflation_floor: A FLOOR OF 1 IS APPLIED TO THE VARIANCE-INFLATION FACTOR so the adjustment can never NARROW an interval below the unadjusted one. That guard is the recognised modification for exactly this instability, and its existence is evidence the small-k behaviour is a KNOWN problem with KNOWN handling rather than a novel judgement.
house_rule_interval_2026_08_18.no_rule_is_decided_here: The house rule is REML with Hartung-Knapp below k=10, settled days ago. Whether it means ALWAYS or WITH A FLOOR AT k=3 is a decision about this corpus, not a computation, and it has been referred rather than taken. BOTH INTERVALS STAND ON THIS PAGE UNTIL IT IS MADE. Nothing is unpublished and no reader is left with only the narrower one.
house_rule_interval_2026_08_18.what_this_means_for_this_pool: THE SIGNIFICANCE SURVIVES THE STRICTER INTERVAL. This pool is BETTER ESTABLISHED than its published interval alone conveys -- the finding holds under the more conservative of the two defensible methods. Recorded as prominently as the reverse case, because a strengthened result is a result.

r21_seasonal_first_12m.estimand_established_does_not_cover_the_: READ THIS BESIDE `estimand_established`. That flag records that every contributing trial measures the SAME QUANTITY. It records NOTHING about what that quantity was measured AGAINST -- whether the comparators are of one kind, whether each comparison was randomised, whether it was concurrent. The two questions were never separated. Named as P48 in PAGE-STANDARD.md v1.21.0 and swept by scripts/audit_mixed_contrast_pools.py.

In the first two rounds it was CORRECT: the object's own stated question demanded the same follow-up window, so the pool contradicted its own criterion. That criterion was invented here, was stricter than the Handbook, and has been withdrawn -- and the question no longer imposes it. THE HANDBOOK DOES NOT SUPPLY A TEST THAT SETTLES THIS. Section 10.10.1 asks that a synthesis be undertaken only where participants, interventions, comparisons and outcomes are judged sufficiently similar to be clinically meaningful, and that judgement is the review authors' -- a low I-squared is not a substitute for it. An earlier version of this text called the combination of same-measure and low heterogeneity 'the Handbook's actual test', which was the same overclaim already withdrawn in two other fields and is withdrawn here. What it crosses is in the uniformity table, what it survives is in the sensitivity table, and a reader who judges the windows too far apart has both cohorts printed separately.
handbook.conformance: Section 10.8 makes the rate ratio the effect measure for rate data and sanctions combining log rate ratios by the generic inverse-variance method. the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.chapter: 13 (bias due to missing results in a synthesis)
the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.finding: Chapter 13 nowhere recommends excluding a non-pre-specified result from the primary synthesis. Its recommended handling is DETECTION (13.3.1.3, comparing study plans against available results), a RISK OF BIAS JUDGEMENT using the ROB-ME tool (13.3.5), and SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS (13.3.4.6) -- not exclusion.
the_handbook_does_not_require_exclusion.and_a_distinction_that_matters: Chapter 13 and ROB-ME address results MISSING from a synthesis. Our case is the opposite direction -- a result PRESENT that was never pre-specified -- which is why section 8.7 is the correct instrument and Chapter 13 is the adjacent one. Section 8.7 says so itself: it 'does not address bias due to selective non-reporting (or incomplete reporting) of outcome domains that were measured and analysed by the trial authors'.

sensitivity_analysis_authority.verbatim: 'Sensitivity analyses should be used to examine whether overall findings are robust to potentially influential decisions.'

authority.the_conservative_principle: WHERE THE HANDBOOK LEAVES A CHOICE, TAKE THE OPTION THAT DOES NOT MOVE A RESULT TOWARD SIGNIFICANCE BY OUR OWN DECISION. An analytic choice of ours that STRENGTHENS our own conclusion needs a stronger justification than one that weakens it. Here the direction decides on its own: a wrong inclusion leaves a null intact, while a wrong exclusion publishes a positive result we created.
authority.how_this_was_verified: The ruling to adopt this reading came from the author. An author's agreement is not a source, so both propositions that would OVERTURN it were tested before it was applied: (1) does the Handbook place a non-pre-specified outcome under ELIGIBILITY? Chapter 3 says the opposite and discourages outcome-based exclusion. (2) is it explicit that such results should be EXCLUDED from primary synthesis? Chapter 13 recommends detection, a risk-of-bias judgement and sensitivity analysis instead. Both fail; the Handbook is more emphatic than the ruling.

gate_dissent.question: Should a pooled point estimate for this outcome be published at all, given that the object itself says its contributors do not estimate one common quantity?
gate_dissent.openai_family_position: It should not. The caveat does not make the pooled point and its efficacy percentage a meaningful estimate; it confirms the opposite, and publishing the number is misleading even when labelled exploratory.
gate_dissent.google_family_position: It is acceptable as published. The outcome is adequately caveated, it states plainly that the contributors share neither a follow-up window nor a regression model, and it is not presented as a real answer.
gate_dissent.resolution: RESOLVED IN FAVOUR OF THE OPENAI FAMILY, and not by preferring one reviewer to the other. The disagreement was referred to the Cochrane Handbook, version 6, and the Handbook settles it twice over: the two contributing estimates are different EFFECT MEASURES under sections 10.8 and 10.9, for which the Handbook provides no conversion, and the heterogeneity sat in the 'considerable' band of section 10.10.2, where section 10.10.3 explicitly offers 'do not do a meta-analysis'. The pooled point, its interval and its efficacy percentage have therefore been REMOVED. The google family's position -- that the caveat was adequate -- is recorded here because it was reasonable and because a record that only keeps the winning argument is not a record. What survives is what the Handbook does support for these data: the per-cohort estimates, and a by-vaccine stratum for each, presented as a narrative comparison rather than as a combined number.
gate_dissent.authority: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, version 6, sections 10.6, 10.8, 10.9, 10.10.2 and 10.10.3.

resolved_2026_08_21.the_text_that_decides_it: RoB 2 guidance 2019, Box 4, signalling question 1.1: "Answer 'No information' if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized." And section 4.4: "A judgement of low risk of bias requires that the trial has an adequate method of concealing the allocation sequence from those involved in enrolling participants, and there are no concerns about generation of the allocation sequence." Cochrane Handbook 6.5 section 8.3 names the domain's three components.
resolved_2026_08_21.why_this_is_not_an_adjudicated_dispute: A blind second assessor from a different model family disagreed with this domain on 89% of judgements across 22 topics. THAT WOULD ORDINARILY BE A DISPUTE TO ADJUDICATE. It is not one: the tool's own text names this exact evidential situation -- a bare statement that a study was randomised -- and prescribes the answer. The second assessor is not being deferred to; the guidance is being applied.
resolved_2026_08_21.what_the_registry_gives_and_does_not: A ClinicalTrials.gov design module records `allocation: RANDOMIZED`. It carries no sequence-generation method and no allocation-concealment mechanism. The original judgement's own note said so before scoring LOW.
resolved_2026_08_21.how_this_maps_to_the_tool_s_algorithm: The tool maps 'No information' on 1.1 and 1.2 with no baseline concern to a DOMAIN judgement of SOME CONCERNS. This project writes NO_INFORMATION on the domain when it could not be judged from the sources read, and caps the OVERALL at SOME_CONCERNS. Same place, and it keeps 'we could not judge this' distinguishable from 'we judged it and had concerns'.
resolved_2026_08_21.what_does_not_change: NO OVERALL RATING AND NO GRADE CERTAINTY MOVES. All 51 judgements were already capped at SOME_CONCERNS or HIGH by another NO_INFORMATION domain.
resolved_2026_08_21.what_would_close_it_properly: The trial publications or protocols, which carry sequence generation and concealment. Neither was read. Until one is, LOW is not available on this domain for any result in this corpus.

A second review indexed the same year states EIGHT (PMID 42001650) -- equal to ours. Class 82: on the larger of the two we are lower, and on neither is the trial set named, so both are COUNTED AND NOT IDENTIFIED. THE UNITS MAY NOT BE THE SAME. This object counts at the level of the RANDOMISED COHORT and records, in its own scope decisions, SEVEN cohorts whose further reports at longer follow-up were deliberately set aside as second reports of one study -- Handbook 4.6.1, 'Studies (not reports) as the unit of interest'. A review counting STUDIES as publications would count some of those separately. THAT IS A HYPOTHESIS AND NOT A FINDING: neither review names its set, so whether their eleven includes reports our rule merges HAS NOT BEEN ESTABLISHED. It is recorded because everywhere else in this corpus a lower count has had no stated reason at all. KEEP THE TWO VACCINES APART. Both published reviews put RTS,S and R21 in one review; this object holds nine separate outcome blocks and pools across vaccines in none of them. The vaccines differ in adjuvant, antigen dose and schedule, and their reported efficacies differ substantially. This is a scope difference, not an arithmetic disagreement, and no number here contradicts a number there. STATED SO THE COMPARISON IS NOT READ AS STRONGER THAN IT IS. Two records were appraised against their abstracts out of 28 matched and 28 read; no included-study table was opened and no full text was retrieved. No quantity of theirs was matched to a quantity of ours closely enough to call it agreement or disagreement, and none is claimed.

manuscript.introduction:
This review asks: For each of the two malaria vaccines separately, what is the efficacy against clinical malaria across the randomised cohorts that report the SAME EFFECT MEASURE for clinical malaria, aligned on every dimension the sources permit and crossing the rest with each difference named on the pool that crosses it -- and where does that differ from the published synthesis of the same literature? The question does NOT claim these cohorts estimate identical quantities. Each pool records whether they do, and neither of them does.

It pools 2 randomised trials, against rabies vaccine.

The outcomes pooled are R21 with the HIGHER Matrix-M adjuvant dose, the formulation carried into phase 3, given seasonally: time to first clinical malaria episode over the first year after the primary series; R21/Matrix-M, standard age-based administration: time to first clinical malaria episode over the first year after the primary series; RTS,S/AS01 with a booster, children: rate of ALL clinical malaria episodes over the full trial follow-up; RTS,S/AS01 with a booster, young infants: rate of ALL clinical malaria episodes over the full trial follow-up; RTS,S/AS01 primary series, children: rate of the first or only clinical malaria episode per person-year over the first year after the third dose; RTS,S/AS01 given alongside the routine immunisation schedule, infants: ratio for all clinical malaria episodes to nineteen months, of a type the source does not name.

Everything in this paragraph is derived from stored fields and none of it is authored. The interpretive sentences that follow are marked as drafts and are the author's to replace.

what_this_review_does_not_publish_2026_0: WHAT THIS REVIEW DOES NOT PUBLISH. This review also examined seven outcomes for which no pooled estimate is published: R21/Matrix-M, standard age-based administration: time to first clinical malaria episode over the first year after the primary series (k=1), which is not pooled; RTS,S/AS01 with a booster, young infants: rate of ALL clinical malaria episodes over the full trial follow-up (k=1), which is not pooled; RTS,S/AS01 primary series, children: rate of the first or only clinical malaria episode per person-year over the first year after the third dose (k=1), which is not pooled; RTS,S/AS01 given alongside the routine immunisation schedule, infants: ratio for all clinical malaria episodes to nineteen months, of a type the source does not name (k=1), which is not pooled; RTS,S/AS01 without a booster, phase 2b: time to first clinical malaria episode over a mean follow-up shorter than a year (k=1), which is not pooled; RTS,S/AS01, seasonal administration, against seasonal chemoprevention rather than against an inactive control (k=1), which is not pooled; The two vaccines side by side on recurrent clinical malaria: SEPARATE estimates in two DIFFERENT effect measures, presented without a combined figure (k=2), which is not pooled. Each of those outcomes is recorded on this review with the reason it was not pooled, and none of them contributes to the estimate reported above (0.2167 at k=2, 0.6372 at k=2). A reader meeting the pooled result should not take it as covering every outcome, or every trial, this review examined. This sentence exists because a second, independent reading -- by a different model family, given the object and the abstract and none of our conclusions -- found that a reader would reasonably conclude the review pools all relevant trials, and that the object does not support that. The withdrawals were already recorded beside the outcomes they concern; they were invisible from the abstract, which is where the impression forms.
